result:
Twice a decade, when the winter moon and an offshore wind struck an unlikely bargain, the bay pulled back far enough to show its bones.

Mara saw it first from her kitchen window while waiting for the kettle to boil. Where there should have been the dark, choppy slate of the morning tide, there was instead a glistening expanse of wet gravel, ridged sand, and long, humped backs of kelp-draped stone. The pier, usually standing knee-deep in whitewater, looked absurdly tall, its barnacled pilings exposed all the way down to the mud.

She abandoned the tea, pulled on her wool coat and heavy rubber boots, and walked down the steep lane to the harbor. 

The air smelled sharply of brine, crushed shells, and cold iron. Already a few gulls were pacing the newly minted shore with an air of bewildered entitlement, poking at stranded starfish and snapping at crabs that hadn't found a deep enough pocket to hide in. Mara stepped off the bottom of the stone slipway and felt the sand give slightly beneath her heels, firm and ribbed like the roof of a whale’s mouth.

Out here, the sound of the town vanished. The rattle of early delivery trucks and the whine of a distant saw were swallowed by the vast, damp hush of the flats. Even the ocean itself was only a thin silver thread humming quietly half a mile away, sulking behind the outer sandbar.

She walked toward the skeletal ribs of the *Maren*, a herring boat that had dragged its anchor during a November gale forty years before she was born. Usually, only the tip of its iron bowsprit broke the surface at dead low water, a hazard marked by a rusted buoy. Today, the whole hull lay bare. The oak planking had long since rotted away, leaving a cage of blackened timbers filled with silt and bladderwrack. Inside the stern, a pool of trapped seawater held a miniature forest of red algae and a single, very large flounder waiting patiently for the world to right itself.

Beyond the wreck, something stranger emerged from the silt: a straight line of flat granite blocks. 

Mara followed them. They weren't a natural reef. Someone had laid them there, side by side, a century or more ago—an old causeway leading out toward a low island of black rock, or perhaps a cart track to a salt-house that the coastline had slowly chewed up and swallowed. Every winter storm shifted the shore an inch or two; a hundred winters made a new map entirely.

Halfway along the drowned road, she saw another figure standing motionless beside a deep tidal channel. As she drew closer, she recognized Arthur, the retired harbourmaster, wearing an oilskin jacket so stiff with salt it looked as though it could stand up on its own. A canvas bucket hung from his left hand.

"Find anything good?" Mara asked, her voice sounding oddly loud in the open air.

Arthur didn't look up immediately. He was using the tip of a wooden walking stick to nudge a tangle of green weed out of a crevice. "Couple of lead weights," he said. "Half a porcelain plate. Blue willow pattern. Probably fell off a galley table in 1920."

He straightened up, his knees popping softly in the cold, and squinted out toward the distant silver line of the sea. "You don't think about how much junk we drop over the side until the water steps out for a smoke."

"I didn't know there was a road out here," Mara said, gesturing with her chin toward the granite slabs beneath their boots.

"Cartway for the quarry," Arthur said. "Before they built the breakwater up north. My grandfather told me he drove a team of horses across here when he was twelve. Said the water was already lapping the axles by the time they got the stone loaded. Place wasn't meant to stay dry."

They stood together for a moment, watching a small ribbon of water begin to snake its way back up the sandy channel between them and the outer bar. It didn't rush. It simply slid forward, thin as oil, filling in the footprints Mara had left behind her.

"We spend a lot of time trying to keep things where we put them," Arthur murmured, lifting his bucket. "Walls, piers, names carved into benches. Then the moon leans a little closer, and you realize everything's just borrowed."

"Is that supposed to be comforting?"

Arthur smiled, the wrinkles around his eyes deepening like cracks in dry clay. "Depends on whether you're the one holding the broom or the one looking for lost plates."

He tapped his stick against the stone and turned back toward the harbor. "Better head in. Water comes back faster than it leaves, and the mud by the slipway gets greedy once it's wet."

Mara lingered for one more minute. Looking back at the town from the middle of the bay, the houses perched along the bluff looked fragile and bright, painted in yellows and faded blues, smoke curling gently from three or four chimneys. From out here, you could see how narrow the strip of dry land really was—just a thin ledge wedged between the dark woods and the vast, breathing machinery of the sea.

She bent down, picked up a piece of sea glass worn smooth as a river pebble—a pale, milky green—and slipped it into her coat pocket. Then she turned her back on the rising silver thread and walked toward the smoke, following the old stone road home before the water came to claim it again.
